Mr. Gott. Liberal member for South Essex, and Mr. Hepburn, Conservative member for West Elgin, are going to meet in joint debate at St. Thomas a week from Saturday.

Order.

The Journal has referred to
me on another occasion as a Liberal member. I resent the imputation, despite the fact that hundreds of Liberal farmers are to-day supporting our policy of protection for the farmers.

On

With regard to my name appearing as a Conservative member, I want to deny the allegation most emphatically.

I suppose the house will

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In the local papers last night and this morning there is an account of the Liberal caucus, in which to my mind the honour of the house and o; the Speaker is brought into question at least the Speaker is severely criticized for certain restrictions he has placed on the activities of the messengers and for other reasons. This tends to hold His Honour up to the country as a man who needs discipline by a party caucus. As a member of this house I protest most emphatically against any caucus, whether Liberal, Tory or U.F.A., attempting to discipline His Honour the Speaker, and so holding him up to contumely. The reports to which I have alluded in both local papers appear under the heading, "Members kicked against the Speaker's ruling and the Speaker's action." Such accounts tend to undermine the prestige of His Honour the Speaker and to create an impression that he may 'be subject to influence in regard to his decisions, the value of which as a consequence may be very seriously impaired. I want to say, sir, that you were elected Speaker by all the members of the house, and that you are the servant, not of the Liberal party but of the whole house. One of the matters brought into question was the fact that you, sir, had given orders to the messengers of this house that they should not supply liquor to members of the house.
No.

That, I understand, was one of the orders. I wish to say, sir, if that is true, that I support such action on your part. But I have full confidence in the impartiality of Mr. Speaker, and I resent the impression that has been created.

May I ask where the question of privilege comes in? An unconfirmed report in the press is cited by the
hon. gentleman, and I fail to see the question of privilege. A few days ago a very serious accusation appeared in the press against some

hon. members of this house and the matter was not allowed to be discussed. I fail to see where the hon. member who is protesting has been injured in any way.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I say to my hon.
friend that I was present at the caucus to which he has just referred, and the one comment of caucus was upon the publicity that had been given to certain instructions issued by Mr. Speaker, which caucus felt had created a wrong impression abroad with respect to certain matters alleged to be transpiring in these houses of parliament. As a matter of fact there was not criticism of Mr. Speaker's instructions; there was no reflection upon Mr. Speaker. The one criticism that was made-and it was made with respect to this House of Commons and this parliament-was that the public would get an entirely wrong impression as to what is transpiring in these buildings, from the publicity that had been given certain instructions upon which the newspapers have put their own interpretation. The thought of caucus was that the committee on internal economy might very well take up that matter with Mr. Speaker, but I find that that committee has no authority whatever in this respect. I would take advantage of the present discussion to suggest that Mr. Speaker might meet with a committee of this house to discuss certain matters that relate to the House of Commons-not to the government but to this house which manages its own affairs. May I say this with respect to any report that has appeared in the press. Caucuses, as every hon. member knows, are private and secret meetings, and there was a most implicit understanding at this caucus, as there has been at every caucus, that members of caucus were to give no statement whatever to the press as to what might transpire there. Anything, therefore, that appears in the press with respect to yesterday's caucus is without any authority, and what I have read of its proceedings in the press cannot be said to be a correct account.
The fact that the Liberal party itself in the Liberal caucus reprimanded the Speaker for his regulations-

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
With many of the observations made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) every member of this House of Commons must be in accord. But I think it is also apparent that a matter of this kind should be discussed behind closed doors; and if it is agreeable to you, Mr. Speaker, I think 78594-96
that before we open the doors to the public at the next sitting we might discuss the subject that has now been brought to the attention of the house. That would be the more proper course to follow in dealing with the situation that has arisen.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac): I was not present at the caucus, but I entirely disagree with the suggestion of the Leader- of the Opposition (Mr. Bennett).	There is
nothing transpiring in this house or in the building, of which any of us are aware, that would necessitate secret discussion.
It is the practice of the house.

If there is to be discussion let us have it in open house. My only experience of a secret meeting of the House of Commons was some years ago when we held such a session to learn of certain things that were taking place in the war.
We have twice had such a meeting in the last few years.

The questions discussed on that occasion were published in the morning papers before this secret meeting took place, and the subject matter of any secret meeting we might hold here would be public property not many minutes after the opening of the house. I do not think, from my short experience in this house, that anything transpires here which cannot be dealt with openly by the members of the house, with Hansard and the galleries present. I entirely object to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition. I repeat, if we have anything to say, let us say it in public.	*

I am inclined to agree to a great extent with my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). Anything that has transpired within the walls of parliament has been broadcast to the four corners of this country. The orders given by His Honour the Speaker, and the manner in which they were executed, are familiar to all who pay any attention whatsoever to the political situation in this Dominion.
What were the orders?

The orders were published in the newspapers, to the effect that certain messengers should not do certain work, and that certain policemen should patrol corridors on such and such floors of this building. I believe therefore that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Pontiac is quite sound, that no good purpose can be served by having a secret session. On the contrary, too much

importance will be attached to what after all are mere incidents, if we take the extraordinary view that a secret session is necessary. Secret sessions are held, as a rule, only when matters of great importance to the nation are to be discussed, and I submit-

May I correct the hon. gentleman in order that he may not misunderstand me. We are speaking merely of the internal economy of the House of Commons, and the secret session proposed is just such a session as those that have been held twice during the past two years in connection with the approaches to this building. It is not well that matters of internal economy should engage the attention of the public; such matters should be discussed by us before the doors are opened.

I accept my hon. friend's correction and I will go further and say that, if the matter is not important enough to warrant a special session behind closed doors, the house to-day should select from amongst its members a committee to wait upon Mr. Speaker to discuss the whole question with him and to report its findings to the House of Commons as soon as possible. In my humble opinion, the matter can be settled in fifteen or twenty minutes by means of a free, frank and open discussion with His Honour, and the report having been made to the house publicly we ^halt no longer have such a situation as has arisen, of reports in the press giving rise to rumours which are utterly unfounded and which seriously reflect upon the honour of all members of this house.
May I ask t'he hon. gentleman, before he takes his seat, what there is to be settled? I am not clear as to what the question is about.

I will briefly explain it,
although it must be quite clear to everyone. Undoubtedly the hon. member must have heard about the matter from conversation with other members. The question has reference to certain orders which have been issued, and to the publicity which has been given to those orders, and I think that question can be settled by discussion with the Speaker.

After a fairly long experience in this
house, I believe that in every instance I can recall where a matter of internal economy has been mentioned it has always been mentioned behind closed doors before the opening of the house. The very first day I sat in the House of Commons the late Sir Charles Hib-bert Tupper mentioned the question of the allocation of rooms as between the two parties

in the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker Brodeur immediately said the point should be discussed behind closed doors on the following day. On at least half a dozen occasions during the last thirty years a similar course has been followed, and I think that is the course which should be pursued now. That is parliamentary practice, and I see no reason for departing from it.

I do not think, that is altogether
the opinion of the house, and I should like to protest against this closed door policy. Certain charges, whether founded or unfounded, have been broadcast by the press. These charges are not made against particular individuals but are made in a vague sort of way which leaves any member of the bouse liable to suspicion. I do not think that is fair to hon. members. Further, the very appointment of a committee such as has been suggested, under these circumstances would be more or less of a reflection upon the decision of the Speaker, and some of us do not want to see anything of that kind take place. Whatever the opinions of the members of the house may be with regard to certain practices, I submit that no one member can act along the lines which have been followed in the past without involving the standing of all the members in this house, against this any member has a right to protest.
I suggest that perhaps we might find a way out of the difficulty by appointing a sort of house committee such as exists in a good many clubs, not to deal with this particular matter at this time but rather as a support

to the Speaker. I quite understand that there are certain difficulties which have made it very hard for the Speaker to act and take the entire responsibility for his actions without at least consulting some of the members in order to obtain their views as to what is proper in the circumstances. I do not think such a committee would discipline the Speaker at all. It would be a means by which various members of the house could make their complaints known to the Speaker in order to obtain that free discussion which is necessary.
With regard to the particular matter now under consideration I would protest against it being decided behind closed doors. If liquor has been carried by messengers, as I understand to be the case, I for one would like to see that practice cease; I do not think that is the work of a messenger of this house.

In view of the knowledge
which I have just gained that the rules do not provide for such a committee as I have suggested, I beg to withdraw my suggestion.
Mr. COOTE.:	It is with a good deal of
hesitation that I rise to take part in this discussion, because it seems to me entirely out of order. However, I am not going to miss this opportunity of pressing for the appointment of what I would call a house committee. For years I have thought such a committee should be appointed.

I am just told that you,

members of the house will feel that Your Honour is the presiding officer of the house and that we should be quite prepared, after what has been said, to leave it to your own judgment, Mr. Speaker, to decide what fur-78594- 96J
ther step it may be advisable to take. I think we might proceed now with the business of the house.

I have no objection to
discussing this matter right now, but in deference to the opinions which have been expressed I shall wait, not until Monday, because, Monday morning I must attend the funeral service of a dear friend of mine in Montreal, but until Tuesday next when, behind closed doors, I will be ready to explain these two orders which were given ir good faith for the protection of the dignitj and the privileges of the house.

I do not want to prolong the debate, but I would like to remind hon. members that it always has been the custom of this house that before the doors are opened any member may bring up any question concerning the internal economy of the house before the ordinary business is taken up. That has been the custom for many years; I could cite many instances where that has been done before the doors were declared open.

Before this question is
left perhaps you, Mr. Speaker, might ask the clerk of the house to give the names of the members of the Internal Economy Commission already appointed, for the benefit of those hon. members who apparently are of the opinion that such a committee does not exist.

Early in the session
a message was read to the house from His Excellency the Governor General appointing four ministers of the crown as members of the Internal Economy Commission, but that commission deals only with the financial matters of this department. It must be remembered that this is a department, and I want the house to understand that as Speaker of the house I am head of a department which employes about 500 people. Under the Civil Service Act the Speaker is, just as much as any minister of the crown, the head of his department. Therefore, when the Speaker gives orders, they must be obeyed. On Tuesday next I will ask hon. members to stand by their Speaker if his instructions are in conformity with the privileges, the honour and the dignity of the house.

I would like to direct the
Speech oj W. H. Moore

attention of the government to a press report of a meeting held last night, which was addressed by Mr. W. H. Moore, chairman of the tariff board. In that speech Mr. Moore uses language which I regard as strictly political and which would result in any civil servant being dismissed under the provisions of the order in council which was approved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and adopted during the regime of Sir Robert Borden. Mr. Moore said:
"We, as the tariff board, should not be left with this tariff problem, nor should those on parliament hill be asked to saddle the whole burden," Mr. Moore observed. "One thing the tariff board has done and that is that it has brought out from day to day the different situations which you people have to face on election day for whatever interpretation you place on them, that is your responsibility."
"There is a conflict of tariff opinion in the United States," Mr. Moore said. "We have a clearer vision of what is going on in the states to-day than we have perhaps of what is taking place at home. But American standards of living cannot be increased by making food dearer. The farmers there have come out boldly with their demand, 'We want dearer food/ but in no case was the demand stated more boldly nor baldly than by the sugar beet farmers, who are asking $6 for sugar, when it is now $4.70."
In reference to the dairy industry, he said:
We hear a lot that our imports of New Zealand butter are increasing and our exports of butter are decreasing. That does not necessarily mean, however, that our dairy is dying; only that it is taking another form in the export of milk and milk products.
I ask the government what is to be done with a civil servant, a servant of the Department of Finance, as the minister said last night, who goes out and carries on political propaganda within sight of the walls of parliament.

The house is entitled to some definite information in a matter of this kind which appears in the report of the hearing before the tariff commission, more especially in view of the fact that this appears to be an enterprise owned by Canadians which is giving employment to Canadians in a Canadian town or city and which had recited the circumstances under which it sought to avail itself of a tariff to enable it, not to exploit an industry but to place it on an equal basis with competition from across the border, asking no favours, but merely to be placed on even terms of competition. I remind the minister that his political chairman of his political board, in the blister copper inquiry where it appeared ;hat raw copper left Canada, went to the United States to be refined and then had to be bought by Canadians at an excess over the price at which United States could buy the same copper for, was good enough to say that Canadians should be placed on terms of equality with respect to competition under such conditions. Mr. Gravestock in his memorandum asks only that his company should be placed on terms of equality with respect to competition: that they should be given an even chance in competition. The minister

says: Look what I am doing for you: I am putting stearic acid on the free list. This is not mentioned in the hearing. Is this the method of compromise to be adopted? The amount involved is small, but the method is one of far-reaching consequence. It represents the difference between the Liberal party and the party with which I am associated. In one instance the government are willing to make a compromise for power, for the purpose of retaining their seats on the treasury benches, without regard to the welfare of Canadian industry. The minister thinks he is going to serve the public by sitting down secretly without Mr. Gravestock, without Mr. Wilson, without any representative of this industry being present, and saying: I will put stearic acid on the free list and not place the manufacturers of crayon upon such terms as, it is claimed in the brief that was submitted to the minister, will enable it to compete successfully with the United States industry. In other words, Canadian industry is to be destroyed in order that more employment may be given to people of the United States and Canadians may be put out of a job. That is the policy the minister has enunciated in his budget if it means anything, and if it does not mean that, it means nothing.

I see from the other
brief which the minister has submitted, reference No. 96-and I fancy this is the first application-the application was for an increase in the duty. There is in the brief one rather significant statement which seems to have been accepted as a statement of fact as it existed: that is, that in the United States the selling price of a certain line of crayons was $7.20, while the selling price of the same article in Canada made by the same United States firms was $6.50. It was asked that a dumping duty be applied and it is stated by Mr. Darby that the dumping duty on that particular lot of crayons would be 16 cents, making the Canadian price $6.66, duty added, while at the same time the price maintained by these United States manufacturers in their own market was $7.20. This clearly indicates the effort, and the successful effort, on the part of United States manufacturers to dump their products in Canada and to destroy competition on the part of any industry in this country. The cost of production in Canada for the same article is pointed out in this brief to be $6.20, allowing them only 46 cents as a margin for selling over the cost of production if they meet the United States price. It strikes me that there is a condition of facts which Should call for some action upon the part of the government.

If a. 16 cent dumping duty is not sufficient to enable the Canadian manufacturer to have at least fair terms, then impose a dumping duty that is sufficient, because it is clear that in this instance the United States manufacturer is using Canada as a dumping ground. He will not cut the price in his own country, though there is evidently competition there, because there are ninety-five concerns engaged in this line of manufacture; but he will cut the price in the Dominion of Canada where it is sought to establish another independent industry. It is to the interest of the United States manufacturer to say: No, we will dump our goods and cut the price to such a point that you cannot manufacture, but the moment you cease manufacturing in Canada, then you will pay the higher price. Surely that is a situation that calls for some action. Has t'he minister had any report upon that phase of the case? Did the official of his department, in the memorandum he has submitted, draw that to the minister's attention? Because it is very clearly set out in his brief. Moreover, these statements seem to be accepted as facts by the board, as well as by Mr. Deachman, Mr. Darby and the applicants, so I assume they are thoroughly substantiated.

While this incident may
seem trivial in itself, it becomes very important because of the policy of the government which is here displayed. Here is a company that is given a concession by the government, and neither the tariff board nor the minister himself has yet shown that the company needs any concession. Not a single thing has been placed before the house to show the need of any concession or to show that this industry needs protection. There is another thing, and that is that the government, by this proposal, is impairing the revenues without in any way aiding the industry from the point of view of the workman, or from any other point of view. I cannot help looking at this incident from no other standpoint than this, that the tariff on this item is used as a bargaining point between the politicians and the manufacturer; it absolutely comes down to that. This company enjoys a monopoly, and nothing has been presented to show that the industry needs help, and so I say it comes down simply to a bargaining point for some reason or other. This is what I protest against, and it is what this budget in particular shows all the way through. It puts the burden on the shoulders of the people, and the government for that very reason is willing to impair the revenues of the country so long as the
whole burden goes on the consumer. I protest against this whole thing.

The copper situation
would probably explain that as clearly as it could be explained. We are shipping blister copper and copper matte out of this country, and when our people want to buy copper rods they are forced to purchase from the Copper Export Company of the United States which sets a rate of a quarter-cent per pound higher to foreigners than to their own people. The rseult is that the Canadian people have to buy refined copper made from their own blister copper at a quarter-cent per pound increase in domestic price. This means they have to pay $5 per ton more than their competitors in the United States. The government is encouraging the shipment of blister copper out of this country and the importing of the fabricated article. The same thing applies to asbestos. I wonder if the minister realizes that there are 250,000 men, women and children employed in the fabrication of raw asbestos in the United States exported from Canada. We sell our raw material at between $50 and $70 per ton and purchase the fabricated material at between $900 and $1,000 per ton. As the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) has pointed out, there is an increasing and improving mineral production, and it is the duty of the government to encourage and not to discourage that condition. The people are complaining that they are being deprived of employment in this country. We are simply digging in the rock and getting out these minerals, putting 
them in a smelter and getting the blister and matte, and then shipping it out in carload lots, and the people are forced to follow the raw material in order to obtain employment.
If I am permitted to anticipate the next item, I would ask the minister to teM us what is going to happen when we develop our aircraft industry and then have no chronometers and compasses made in this country.
You will never learn to make them by increasing the production cost.

We will learn to make
them the same as they learned to make them in Germany. There was once a day in Germany and the United States when they imported all these things from England and the same specious argument the hon. gentleman now makes was made when industries were established in these countries. We will never encourage industry by increasing the cost of production. The cost of steel rails in the United States was at one time higher than in England, Germany or Belgium; but the United States and Germany said:	We are
going to promote industry at home to give employment to our own people. They did so, and the result was that thousands of men, who were formerly denied employment, were employed in fabricating thousands of articles, and encouragement was given to their own industry. We do not ask protection; we ask equality of opportunity: we want an equal chance. I cannot understand Canadians; I cannot understand the hon. member for Weyburn; I cannot understand those who appear before the board and take the attitude they do, and I cannot understand the minister when he permits himself to become a party to a transaction which denies to Canadians the right to fabricate their own raw material into the finished article and to give employment to our own people. Are we to be economic slaves or not?-that is the question. If my hon. friend has his way, we will continue to be economic slaves, because every day that passes under present conditions makes us so more and more. We are importing $1,000,000 a day in iron and steel products; we are the greatest customer of the United States Steel Corporation to-day, and this country with a little intelligence, a little determination and a little less fear on the part of those occupying the treasury benches, of the hon. member for Weyburn and those he represents, would be able to stop this at once. What is happening is that we are shipping out our raw material in continually increasing quantities just as

we are doing now in regard to this item of platinum. Then we are buying back the fabricated, highly refined article the manufacture of which gives employment to thousands of people, and we use it and think we are prosperous. That is what is going on in Canada and the hon. gentleman knows it. Will he read the economic history of Germany or the United States or any other country? What about the industrial life of England to-day?

A country that
under free trade was able to finance the greater part of the war.

Surely the hon. gentleman knows what it is costing the poor English taxpayer to-day to pay interest on the money which England borrowed from the United States. Surely he knows the burden on them is so great they are staggering under it; that their industrial life has been threatened at every point, and that the only hope they have is by safeguarding it. I crossed over there only a few years ago and there were no customs men such as we see now at Dover. They are there now gathering up the Swiss watches, automobiles, chronometres, everything else for duty purposes, to endeavour to safeguard industry for one purpose and one only, namely, that the English workman shall have an equal chance with the continental workman to live. When we ask that Canadians shall have a chance to live, .we want them to live in Canada and not in the United States. We want them to live here, eat our wheat, our vegetables, pay taxes in Canada and become part of the life of this country. That is what we are trying to do, and the hon. gentleman knows it. If we continue to do as we are doing, we shall be merely hewers of wood and drawers of water, shipping out the raw material, matte, blister copper, raw material, whether it be pulpwood or cordwood or whatever it may be, and bringing back the highly finished product. Look at the importations of paper. Look at the future. Before this budget ends, the minister will find before him a record of material we are buying which should be made at home and because we are doing this we have lost 600,000 Canadians in the last five years. That is the condition with which we are confronted, and that is the reason for it. This is the principle once more, and the minister has the hardihood to put into tariff items the words " not made in Canada." Is it always to be " not made in Canada"? Is that condition always to continue? That is the problem which confronts the country. It requires courage; it requires more than that;
it requires an appreciation of a problem that is not to be dealt with by temporizing expedients to maintain power. The government must be prepared, if need be, to sacrifice power for Canada and Canadians, and as long as they talk platitudes about the cost of production and free trade, we know quite well what will happen-the same temporizing tariff measures, the same effort to do what has been done in days gone by. Not made in Canada! Of course they were not; there were no steel rails made in Canada once. There were no steel rails made in the United States once. In Lincoln's time every steel rail in the United States came from some other country. But they encouraged their workmen so as to put the development of their country on an equality with that of Germany, and now' they can meet the world in producing steel rails. The same is true in regard to other matters.
The position is this: Shall we continue as we are doing? That is the real issue before the Canadian people. The minister is here continuing to aid and persistently abet the export of raw material, and then he slips over it by adding the words "not made in Canada." Does he remember that there were times in Canada when we did not grind flour except between two stones in the little grist mills? We had no roller patents, but we got them. Are we to continue in the old way? When the hon. member for Cariboo put before us the conditions with respect to the black sand in British Columbia, with respect to nickel in the Sudbury district, with respect to development now going on in Quebec, he harks back to a time when none of this development had taken place, the time when twenty-one years ago the hon. member for South Wellington and he supported the same policies, and he says: Let us continue. That is conservatism gone mad; that is Toryism. But the conservatism, the Toryism you find on this side is reflected in that single verse of Tennyson:
That man's a true conservative
That lops the mouldered branch away.
The mouldered branch is this played-out idea that when this country reaches a certain stage of development, we shall cling to old conditions and not encourage new production, new manufactures. That is the situation to which we are directing the attention of the minister this afternoon, not because this particular item is important, but because the principle makes for the very economic life of Canada.

It seems to me that the mouldered branch is protection. If

Why should it be needed?

Let me give a personal
experience for the benefit of my hon. friends. While in New York I was discussing various matters with a gentleman, an intimate associate of the late President Roosevelt and closely identified with the operations of some of the big financial concerns over there. He made a strong argument to me as a basis for bringing Canada and the United States closer together. He proposed that Canada should adopt the policy of exporting her raw materials and purchasing the finished products from the United States, and he used this expression. He said, " Mr. Stevens, if we would join with you-speaking of Canada-with your raw materials and with our great industrial establishments, we could beat the world." I said, " Hold on a minute, Mr. So-and-so." Then I expounded to him the views which I have tried to place before the house this afternoon and on other occasions regarding the destiny of Canada. My argument to him, and my argument to my hon. friends from Weyburn and Rosetown, is that instead of Canada simply sending her asbestos, 82 per cent of her copper, and her platinum to the United States and to Wales-and this applies also to other of our raw materials-instead of continuing to do that I argued with him that Canada should build up industrial and manufacturing concerns based upon these raw resources, and I carried my argument through as well as I could to its conclusion. When I ended, that gentleman said to me, " If I were a Canadian I would take exactly the

same position. But I want to tell you that the chief concern of the American financial interests to-day is to secure a larger and still larger control of Canadian raw resources to replace the exhaustion of our own resources." The Americans come up and seize control- legally of course-of that great raw resource, and it is being sent down to the United States. As I intimated to-day, 250,000 people, if I am not mistaken, directly and indirectly are being sustained out of raw material for which we get the comparatively paltry sum of seven million dollars a year.

We have the material, we have the opportunity of developing the manufacture of the class of articles in which this is used, and we are not taking advantage of that opportunity. The minister knows, as well as he knows he is in his seat, that I am enunciating sound economics for Canada, but he does not turn a hand or move a finger to give effect to such a policy in this regard. speechtext: Or " safeguarding industry."

liberty to use any pseudonym, as the Prime Minister referred to our own, that he likes. He may invite the member for Weyburn to collaborate with him and call it free trade. I know that a great deal of eloquence has been directed from this side to the Minister of Finance this afternoon, and he is probably laughing up his sleeve at us, thinking that we have been impressed by the argument on this side. That is all I have to say in that connection.
Let me refer for a moment to something the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) said in regard to the copper situation, which he discussed a moment ago. In my opinion he did not show the worst side of that situation. He showed how the copper was exported from Canada and was under the control of the copper export people of the United States, so that our manufacturers had to buy back the manufactured1 or partly manufactured article-wire and rods, or the material to make into wire and rods. They have to apply to the export company for their raw material. This Canadian manufacturing company actually makes an application to the American exporting company for 1,000 tons of copper, and for that copper the Canadian company must pay $5 per ton more than is paid by an American company. That is not the worst feature of it, however; they go further than that. When the Canadian company makes application for 1,000 tons of raw copper the American export company says, " We cannot give you 1,000 tons to-day; we can only give you 250 tons and you will have to come back in two weeks, when we will tell you what we can do about the balance." The Canadian company goes back in two weeks and the American company says, "We can give you another 250 tons but we will have to charge you an additional $5 per ton." That is what happens every time the Canadian company goes back for the balance of their order, and I submit

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
that it is about time we found some solution for a condition of this kind. We produce the raw material and send it to the United States to be refined, but when we want to buy it back we are dictated to with regard to the price. How long are we to continue to be treated in this way not only by the United States but by a-ny foreign country? This does not seem to me a reasonable business basis, and I think it is about time the government woke up and applied some remedy to a condition of this kind.

Ever since I came to this house I have been pleading with the present Minister of Finance and with other ministers to take some interest in the ore industry and the mineral production of Canada. I pointed out what Canada was deriving from her one smelter, located at Trail, even though that smelter was operated on a small scale and only taking care of the one mine, and I drew attention to the fact that under present conditions we were losing millions of dollars a year in this way. In the case of nickel in northern Ontario we were simply producing the ore and sending it to the United States; in the case of the other ores, they were sent to Deloro where concentrates were formed, which concentrates were shipped to the United States for further refining and smelting. The minister says there are only small quantities of platinum or other metals shipped out of Canada, but we have no idea what is in these concentrates. However, now we know that we are obtaining platinum and several of these other minerals right in Ontario and t'he northern part of Quebec, and if we do not institute a policy of completing the refining of our metals in our own country we will continue to lose millions of dollars annually.
After all, platinum is only a small matter; for seven years I have pleaded with the minister to consider the question of the treatment of feldspar, which is obtained in Ontario in its finest form. To-day we ship practically all the ore to the United States to be ground, after which it is returned to Canada free of duty, while great quantities are retained in the United States for the development of their great industries, T?he minister has thrown out a gesture to-day, and I ana hoping that it is a promise that he is preparing for the further manufacture of platinum in this country. I hope it is a a promise, because to-day feldspar is being ground by two concerns in Canada, .and we have the whole production in our own hands if we wish to make use of it. These two industries, one in Toronto, and one in Kingston, are now prepared to grind our own feldspar in sufficient quantities to supply the manufacturers of Canada, but the minister has turned them down repeatedly when they have asked for a little protection. I believe he has done so innocently, however, without having been given the information. These firms have assured him that if he will grant them some small protection in order to give them the Canadian market, they are willing to employ twice the number of people they are employing at present. In other words, if he will see that United States manufacturers do not have an opportunity of sending this product to Canada under conditions equal to those Which must be met by the Canadian companies, they will carry on the manufacture of feldspar in our own country and will not increase the price of any article into the production of which it enters. I hope the gesture of the minister indicates a determination that he will deal with the further manufacture of these ores in Canada and that next year he will take cognizance'of the question of feldspar in order that the manufacture of this product may be carried on in Canada.

I serve notice on them now, in the presence of my friends, that if they do not live up to that agreement we will find means of placing them in a position where they will have to do so, or meet competition of the world.
My suggestion to the minister is that 'he take off the excise tax on cars valued at $1,200 or less, no matter where they are made. That is the only way of assuring the people of Canada that these companies will live up to the promise they made in 1926.
Did my hon. friend see the statement by Mr. Campbell of the Ford company a few months ago, in which he said his company lost over S60 on every car they turned out last year?

I did not see that statement, but here I have a statement made to the house by the minister three years ago, when he said these people would have to live up to this promise or he would place them in a position where they would have to meet the competition of the world. I charge that they have not lived up to that promise, and I ask the minister now to tell the house whether he is not convinced that he should remove this excise tax from American-made cars in order to keep the promise he made the house in 1926.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend forgets that
according to the statement the majority of these people have lived up to that promise. There is also a question of revenue involved, which has to be looked into carefully. These other companies which he alleged are not living up to the promise are in competition with the companies which have lived up to it, and I am sure the people will not buy these cars if prices are too high.

The minister should not attempt to get out of his promise in that way. [Mr. Coote.l
He did not say that if certain of the manufacturers lived up to the agreement it would be all right, even though other manufacturers did not do so; he said if they did not all live up to it he would do a certain thing, and I think the house took it for granted that that was what he was going to do.
That is out of date; that was last year.

No, that was three years
ago. Perhaps the Minister of Finance is like some people who, when they get on in years, find their memory of what happened long ago better than their recollection of what happened in the immediate past. I am trying to find in Hansard a statement made by the minister in 1926, when it was suggested to him that if he were going to put this into force he should place in the act a stipulation that if the companies did not live up to the agreement the government would reintroduce the excise tax on Canadian-made cars. At page 4136 of Hansard for 1926 I find that the hon. member for Rosetown asked the following question:
If we are going to pass this amendment to-night I would like to know if it contains a provision that if at any time it is proved to the satisfaction of the government that this rebate of excise tax is not passed on to the consumer, the tax will at once again be imposed.
The minister's reply was as follows:
To do that it would be necessary to give the governor in council the right to increase taxation, and that is not good legislation.
It seems to me now that it would have been good legislation.
We have, however, the right to reduce taxation, and if they do not live up fairly to this agreement we have the right to reduce the excise tax to all the trade of the world.
Mr. Evans:	Will that be inserted in the
bill?
Mr. Robb:	It is not necessary.
I am rather convinced from the answer given a moment ago by the minister that it really was necessary, and perhaps the house was derelict in its duty in not insisting that that be done. I have a high personal regard for the minister, as I had at that time, and from the statement he made that night I believed him to be in earnest in this regard; I thought if these men did not live up to the agreement, as soon as the matter was brought to his attention he would remove the excise tax on imported cars as well. Is not that the impression which anyone would gather from reading the remarks which I have quoted from Hansard? I do not wish unduly to delay the committee on this matter but I think the minister owes it to the committee to state that unless these automobile companies can

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
absolutely prove, by a comparison of the prices of the different models of their cars in Canada with the prices in the United States, that they are not taking advantage of this excise tax, collecting that tax in actual practice and putting it in their 'own pockets, the minister should at once remove the excise tax on all cars. The minister stated:
We have, however, the right to reduce taxation, and if they do not live up fairly to this agreement we have the right to reduce the excise tax to all the trade of the world.
I asked the minister to take this tax off and have the reduction applied to all cars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can answer that quickly
by saying, no. Cars coming from countries with whom we have no preferential trade agreement pay the excise tax when they are valued under $1,200.
Is that tax five per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Five per cent where the value is under $1,200 and ten per cent where the value is over $1,200. Any person who buys a high-priced car, one costing five or six thousand dollars, is able to pay the government a little revenue. If the hon. member were to argue that we should consider raising the limit next year, I might consider that, but it is too late to do anything this year. My hon. friend says that a few companies have not lived up to this agreement, and I will tell him that to-morrow morning I am going to send them a letter enclosing a copy of Hansard and demanding an answer. But why should we lose revenue when the great bulk of the trade is living up to the agreement?

How do you know they
are doing that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They say so, and it has not
been contradicted to-night. I am not here in the interests of the countries who do not give Canada any trade concessions; this legislation is very fair and the government of Canada is obtaining a certain revenue from the high-priced cars, and it all goes towards the liquidation of the national debt.

All I am asking the minister to do is to take the excise tax off all cars under $1,200 regardless of whether or not they are made in Canada. My reason for asking that is the statement made by the minister in 1926, when he persuaded the house to pass this amendment which removed the excise tax on cars valued at less than $1,200, and the realization that certain manufacturers have not lived up to that agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A very limited number.

If the cars valued at $1,200
or under which are produced in Canada are not being sold under the proper terms and at the proper price, I would like the minister to explain to the house just what he meant when he said in 1926:
We have, however, the right to reduce taxation, and if they do not live up fairly to this agreement we have the right to reduce the excise tax to all the trade of the world.
Mr. Evans:	Will that be inserted in the
bill?
Mr. Robb:	It is not necessary.
The house did not consider it was necessary after the Finance minister made that statement. They took it for granted that if the companies mentioned in that letter, and who had given their word to Mr. Russell, authorizing him to write the letter, did not live up to the agreement the minister would place all automobiles valued at less than $1,200 on the same basis. That is the impression which he gave the house. Now he says that as some of the automobile manufacturers have lived up to this agreement, and as he needs this revenue, he is not going to do anything. I suggest that he put them all on the same basis, or that he reinstate the excise tax on Canadian-made as well as on imported cars. If he will not take the tax off all cars valued at less than $1,200, then I suggest that he do that. I now ask the minister if he is willing to put this tax on all cars,, whether or not they are made in Canada? That would be an attempt to make good his word given in 1926.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member is asking
me to break faith with that part of the automobile industry which is living up to this agreement.

What proof have you
of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No one has contradicted that statement.
You have not given any proof of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member must remember that we require revenue.
Never mind the question of revenue; let us take up the other matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When a company is manufacturing, in Oshawa, Ford City, Windsor, Toronto or Regina, oars which come within this regulation, we Obtain a certain revenue from the excise tax. If we removed that excise tax we would be placing the manu-

facturer in the foreign country who might not be giving us any concession on our products, on the same basis as those in countries which were. We would be losing that revenue, and we need the revenue.

The hon. minister is
becoming more and more Conservative.
I think it has been demonstrated that there has been a certain amount of discourtesy shown to the minister by certain automobile -people who did not reply to his letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with that.

I do not want to appear as a defender of any automobile manufacturer, but I would like to put a certain phase of this question before the house. Last year or the year before -the Ford company put out a new car. It took them a long time to get this car on the -market and they introduced it without knowing just what the car was going to cost them. The Ford company in the United States put a price on the car without knowing what it was going to cost them, and they lost $100,000,000 before they could get into production. For the same reason, the Canadian company lost $5,000,000. Is it any wonder that they did not reply to the letter of the minister? If I had been in their place I would have replied by telling the .minister that w-e had lost money on our product and we were only beginning to make money. They are just getting into production, and it seems to me that that is a valid reason why the Ford company did not reply.

I would like to know the price of a Ford coupe in the United States and in Canada. I believe in protecting the Canadian manufacturer, but when I pay $740 for a Ford coupe in Canada and I can go across to a town in the United States, which is three times as far from Detroit as -my home town is from Ford, Ontario, and find that the same car is sold for $200 lees, I begin to wonder what the tariff board are doing. If I were on the tariff board I would want to see that the Canadian purchaser was able to buy that car just as cheaply as the American purchaser. This talk about extra freight is a thing of the past as far as Canada is concerned. We have the right kind of buyers in Canada, because they pay for the articles they purchase. I have worked for different companies long enough to know that they do not lose much money in that way. I would like to know how it is we have to pay $200 more for a Ford car in Canada. What are the tariff

board doing about it? If it is not there for the purpose of giving direct information to the Minister of Finance, I think it is an unnecessary expense. The Minister of Finance of this country is to my mind, bigger than any manufacturing institution either in Canada or the United States, and he is here to protect the Canadian purchaser. I -am a Canadian purchaser, and I know I have been paying $200 more for a Ford coupe in Canada than the same car could have been purchased for in the United States. What is the reason?

As regards the information the Minister of Finance is giving to the committee to-night, it would appear from correspondence I have befo-re me that only two of the automobile firms manufacturing cars in Canada have demonstrated that they have lived up to the understanding of 1926. I am very much surprised at the statement of the minister to-night. Let me say frankly, that prior to to-night I had a very high respect for the word of the minister; but after hearing his explanation respecting this matter, I am coming to doubt whether I was justified in having that high regard for him. Would the Minister of Finance, for instance, wish those of us who met him first when this particular question was brought to the committee who were cooperating with the government at that time, to give to the house all the information that was brought out at that meeting and all the promises he then made to see to it that, if this were granted, the companies would live up to their agreement? So far as I am concerned the statement which the minister has made to-night is actually rubbish in comparison with the statement he then made that he would see that those companies did live up to their agreements. At that time we knew, of course, the government needed support, and we were willing to support them on a policy agreed upon between ourselves. A good deal has been said in different parts of the country as to that agreement between the government and ourselves, but I am free to say that with the exception of this one proposition, the government have lived up to each and every item we agreed to. But the minister to-night has not given the committee one iota of information that would give us even the suggestion of an idea that he had tried to see to it that these companies lived up to their agreement as outlined in a letter by Russell. Is this all the minister has done in the matter-merely write to Russell: when he receives a reply, let it go at that, and, when the committee asks for information, blandly say: "The government needs revenue"? The minister's word is of

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
more importance to the house than the revenue is to the country. I do not want to see this item pass until we get some definite promise from the minister that he will keep his word, will keep the promise he gave and which we honestly believed he would live up to when he first brought that proposal before the committee which was working with the government in that cooperative arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can only repeat to my hon.
friend that the evidence goes to show that I have kept my word. I have written to them all.
Is that all the minister has done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all.
That is nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for North
Wellington has made a statement. I have heard it many times around the country, and* perhaps there is something in it.

Does the minister not
think he- ought to find out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, we have a statement
of a man who knows something about the business. He has not indicated that the charges are wrong. I repeat, that generally speaking, it goes to show that the prices have been fair; that the manufacturers have not been taking advantage of the 5 per cent.

I think the evidence is almost beyond dispute. I have not been able to get the prices of Ford cars this year. I have not seen the Canadian price of a Ford car at the factory in any advertisement this year. It almost seems as if the Ford Company were very careful now not to advertise the factory price of their car, that is, without the sales and excise taxes added. But these are the prices of a year ago, and they have not been disputed. I gave -them on March 6, 1928. The United States price which I shall quote, was taken from a motor magazine published in the United States, giving the factory price of every model of every make of car in the United States. There is no similar magazine in Canada that I have been able to find, and the Canadian prices were all taken from advertisements in Canadian publications. They are the prices without any taxes added in either case so that the prices in the two countries are comparable.

a

I can well remember the
promise which the minister gave in reply to a question I asked him when this matter was under consideration three years ago. Tonight we are face to face with another instance such as I described yesterday where the manufacturer gets all the benefit of a tax reduction and the burden is put on the consumer. I do not know why public men at the head of affairs here should practically prostitute their reputations in making promises like this which are never meant to be kept. It is rather hard to say these things, but we are simply bringing the public life of this country down to a system of bargaining, and something worse, sometimes. It has been plainly shown that the manufacturers have not lived up to the promise given to the minister when this tax was taken off, and I think it is up to the minister himself and his colleagues either to replace the tax or see that the benefit is passed on to the consumer.
As to the statement made here to-night that certain companies are not making profits, I have in my hand the Financial Times for April 5 last, and I find that for the first quarter of 1929 up to March 3l, the Canadian Ford Company made profits amounting to $2,954,600, made up as follows:	January,
$810,000; February, $944,000; March $1,200,000. That undoubtedly goes to show that undue profits are being made by these companies. Surely now we can expect either that this excise tax will be replaced for the sake of getting more, revenue, and the necessaries of life relieved of some of the taxation placed on them, or that the government will see to it that these manufacturers live up to the promise they made.

Mr. Chairman, we have
an extraordinary situation here. In 1926 certain taxes were remitted or cancelled with regard to automobiles. Some members of this house were afraid at the time that the manufacturers would take advantage of that remission and not give the consumer the

benefit. The Minister of Finance promised this house that if they did not give the consumer the benefit, he would see that they were put up against the competition of the world. A year afterwards the matter was again brought up in this house, and an hon. member drew the attention of the Minister of Finance to his promise. The result was that the minister got into communication with the automobile manufacturers and asked them if they had failed to carry out their promise to him. Some of the manufacturers have replied, but in most cases they have given no proof that they have not charged the consumer to the hilt, or that they have passed on to the consumer the benefit of the reduction. Some manufacturers have not even had the decency to reply. The Finance minister to-night says that most of them have replied, but some have not, he admits. The Minister of Finance is the last person in this country who ought to be ignored in the matter of correspondence, and I cannot understand why he and the officials of his department did not go after representatives of these companies who had neglected to reply. It seems extraordinary to me. Again, the Finance minister says: "Oh, well, some of these companies, according to their own statements, have come across and given the consumer the benefit, but I admit that a percentage have not." He might just as well say:	Ninety per cent of the people
of this country are perfectly honest and not ten per cent are rogues, but let them go anyway because ninety per cent are all right. I cannot understand the attitude of the Minister of Finance.
If I understand the position correctly, all export trade is exempt from this tax, is it not?

speechtext: Yes.

Also exports from
countries with which we have trade agreements?

Then how can the

That is administered through
the Department of National Revenue. Their auditors go to the companies and audit their books and accounts. That system is required to establish not only the basis of the Canadian content, but also for export purposes.

How does the minister
arrive at the content of the domestic car in Canada, when the export and the domestic trade must be considered as one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is done through the Department of National Revenue, who have officers making an audit from time to time. Let me say to my hon. friend that some of these companies are not qualifying for export business, because they do not come up to the requirements. The minister does not

I cannot tell my hon. friend

My hon. friend will have to

hon. minister. He has told the house that this is a matter of revenue. I have listened with great attention to what he has been saying this evening, and while he has been treated with great disrespect and discourtesy by the failure of some of the motor companies to answer his letters, when he was making that statement I could not but recall the dramatic stand he took, how he "stood by his guns" down in the theatre before those thousands of Oshawa working men who descended on Ottawa and told them what he was not going to do. Why?

''compliments" to-night.

same part of the country and I do not suppose these little brushes will hurt us. I am prepared to do my part. As I said a few moments ago, I shall write these companies to-morrow, with copies of Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But I submit my hon. friends have not submitted proof that the companies are not living up to their agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have that submitted to the officers to check up, because last session my hon. friend gave figures which he had to correct some weeks afterwards.

On one car only, and as
soon as I found that figure was incorrect,' on a question of privilege I promptly put the matter right. The memorandum I have on this item indicates that it is proposed to amend the present schedule to cover apparatus for sterilizing bulbs, and apparatus for determining the maturity of fruit, in accordance with applications made by the Canadian Horticultural Council. The sterilizing of bulbs consists in the removal of fungus diseases from bulbs and this apparatus is used by bulb growers on the Pacific coast. It is not made in Canada, being imported chiefly from the United Kingdom. The imports are not ascertainable. Fruit pressure testing apparatus is a device used by fruit inspectors. It is imported from the United States and, according to the evidence given at the public hearing, it is not manufactured in Canada. It enters under item 437. The imports are not ascertainable. This latter item is otherwise unchanged.
Is this the machine the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is going to use to spray his motor with?

The
minister has not answered my question. I want to know what agricultural implements come in under the latter provision of this item, "and other agricultural implements, n.o.p.; and complete parts of articles specified in this tariff item." The machine which is called the harvester and which is now known as the combine is being extensively used in western Canada, and comes in at 10 per cent. That is my information from the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This n.o.p. provision is the only item it can come under. My hon. friend has discussed the matter with me and, frankly, I am in sympathy with his point of view. But in the first discussion he did not give me to understand that he also included the motor. But the motor being included, as well as the thresher and the reaper, the matter becomes rather complicated. I have therefore asked the tariff board to investigate my hon. friend's inquiry.
Mr. BENNETT; That is a good way to put it off.

Probably I have received a little more information since the interview I had with the minister. I would ask him to turn to item 445, which relates to mowing machines and harvesters, self-binding or without binders. It is not necessary to read the item at length. It is free under the British preferential tariff, while under the intermediate and the general it is 6 per cent. This whole item was changed in 1924 to cover all harvesting machinery used in Canada. Going into the records with the Commissioner of Customs, I find that this word "harvester" was introduced back in 1897, when some American farmers who were operating in the southern part of the prairies near the Montana border brought over a harvester which was manufactured in California and which at that time was called the harvester. These are not new machines. They have been operating for forty-two years in some sections of the United States, and recently we have found that we can operate them successfully in western Canada. The designation "harvester, without binder" no doubt means the harvester without binding attachment. When this change was made in 1897 it referred to what we now nickname the "combine." There is no doubt that this machine has been wrongly classified; it should come in under item 445. There should be no difficulty in classifying it under that item just because some new implement company calls it a reaper-thresher in order to have something a little different from other companies;

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
that is no reason why this machine should be penalized 4 per cent as compared with other harvesting machinery. Item 447b relates to threshing machines, and the ordinary threshing separator has no motor attached to it. In western Canada to-day we can buy a motor which will operate any threshing machine with a cylinder up to 36 inches for less than $1,200, and that motor enters duty free. Here is the motor in a tractor coming in duty free, while a motor of the same horse-power attached to this particular machine pays a duty of 10 per cent. Right now, while this is before the committee, I think the minister should take steps to have any misconception cleared up with regard to the interpretation of this section It is true that representations have been made that this machine should enter under the 10 per cent rate because it is partly a thresher, but if I took the necessary time I could show that part of the threshing machine is a fanning mill, some of the wheels belong to some other machine, and so on. This classification is not in keeping with the revision of the tariff in 1924, and I hope the minister will take this into consideration.
I might quote a few figures to show what this will mean to us in the west. As farmers in western Canada we must keep 100 per cent efficient or. we cannot make a profit, and this is one of the machines we are compelled to use for economic, reasons. In recent years our help has not been up to the standard of previous years; to-day we cannot get a threshing crew as competent as the crews we had ten years ago; they are also more expensive, so we are compelled to use this machine. Last year the use of these machines increased 611 per cent as compared with 1927; 3,657 of them entered Canada, some of them costing as much as $4,000. If we calculate from the increase in these machines in the last two years, a duty of 4 per cent means a tax of about $1,000,000 on the farmers of the prairie provinces for 1929, and possibly that will amount to $1,500,000. Of course that adds to the revenue of the country but it comes out of the pockets of the producers, who can least afford to pay it. I would like the minister to tell us to-night that from now on this machine, which is not, specificall}'' classified as a combine, will be classified as a harvester, which fully describes it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mv hon. friend has pointed
out the difficulty that it is also classified as a thresher. I asked the Department of National Revenue why this higher rate of duty was imposed, and they referred me to the Customs Act which says that when two rates of duty are applicable the higher rate must prevail. I can only repeat that I have already referred this matter to the tariff board for inquiry and I think they understand that I want to be able to make representations to the government in time to have the matter considered next session. My hon. friend knows that we cannot make these changes rapidly, and he has also said that the motor comes in free already.
No; it pays 10 per cent.

The
motor pays 10 per cent, but that is not the point. The thresher-separator, which comes in under a duty of 10 per cent under section 60 of the Customs Act, is a unit by itself, with no motor attached. The motor which operates that separator, which motor may be in a tractor, comes in free. If we took the motor out of the tractor and attached it to the harvester it would pay a duty of 10 per cent, and that is a wide discrepancy. When the word "harvester" was put in the act in 1897 it covered this particular machine, although of course it has been improved since that time. In the olden days the machine derived its power from a ground wheel, or what we call a bull wheel; there was no motor attached to the machine. However, the machine has been improved; a motor has been attached to it and that motor enters under a duty of 10 per cent, although when the same motor is built into a tractor it comes in duty free.

I am glad the Minister
of National Revenue is in his seat. My friend the Minister of Finance is always asserting to hon. gentlemen to my left his desire to reduce the tariff. Rightly or wrongly a Conservative administration took off the duty on tractors and in 1924, as has been pointed out, the government reduced the duty on farm implements. This particular machine now known as a combine is more accurately described as a harvester; that describes it better than any other word in the English language, because it is a harvester in the true sense of the word. Not only does it cut the grain; it threshes the grain and finishes the job. With this machine you cut the stalks, thresh the heads and as a result of that operation you have the kernels of wheat clean and finished. I first saw one of these machines in Oregon some thirty-one years ago this fall; it was then being pulled by twelve horses, I think.
Was it not twenty horses?

My hon. friend thinks
it was twenty horses, but my memory is that it was pulled by about twelve. Great improvements have been made since that time. I asked what the machine was and I was told
1546	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
that it was a harvester which cut the heads, leaving quite a stand of straw, threshed them, bagged the grain and finished the operation completely.
So I put it to the minister if this is not what he is trying to do: He is trying to get protection by a classification which is at variance with the English language; he is trying to protect his friends by not classifying this machine as a harvester. He is simply using a classification which avoids a word he knows would give offence to his friends behind him-"protection". He says, "We are going to charge 10 per cent on this harvester because it is a combination of many machines, which makes it in every sense a harvester."
I am sorry I was not here at, the commencement of this discussion, but I would like to know what the Minister of National Revenue is being accused of.

According to his colleague, the Minister of Finance, this machine is not classified as a harvester, because as a harvester it would come in under a 6 per cent duty under item 445. In order to afford protection they classify it under another item because there is a motor and something else connected with it. It has to pay 10 per cent because they say it is a threshing machine.
Exactly.
Is it a threshing machine?
It is a part of a threshing machine.

Is it a reaper? It is a combination of both, and therefore a complete harvester. In order to afford protection to their friends, and not having the courage to do it by means of a statute, they apply this classification, and do this violence to the English language. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) smiling.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let us do away with all that protection.

Let us all go to Geneva; here are no threshing machines there.
M.r. ROBB: Does the hon. leader of the jpposition recommend a -lower rate?

I expected that question, but you are a little late. Why does not the hon. minister say, "Will you reduce it or increase it?" It is the old story; neither the Minister of Finance nor his government has the courage to face the situation, and they dodge behind every available excuse in order to make these gentlemen -believe it is not a harvester because it has a motor in it. They

say it has a threshing machine in it, and -also a reaper in it. Of course, it is the combination of all those things which -makes it a harvester. If the Minister of Finance looked at one how would he describe it? He would say, "That is a harvester." Would he say it is a thresher? He would not. Would he say it is a reaper? He would not. Would he say it is a -motor car? He would n-ot. He would say, "It is a harvester," and so would -the Minister of National Revenue.
I would say nothing of the kind.

Because he had ruled the other way, but if he let his intelligence guide him, he would say, "It is a harvester." If he looked at a printing press in his office, which folded the paper, where an older press did not fold the paper, would he call it a printing press or a folder? Of course he would not call it a folder, nor would he call it a dynamo if it were run by electrictiy. I cannot imagine more violence being done to one's sense of what you -might call consistency in the use of the English language. Suppose you go downstairs and look at the dynamo there; you would see there is a belt, brushes and various other things on it. But you would not describe it as a brush, as a turbine or as a belt; you would describe it as a dynamo. My hon. friends get up here and say, "This is not a harvester; this has a motor in it." If the Minister of Justice were not involved in this matter as a colleague of the minister I would leave it to -him to say whether a combination of a thresher, a reaper and a motor would not make a complete harvester.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I will find that -out.

I think he would find
with me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
For the first time this week
the House of Commons appears to be unanimous. Practically ever since the budget was brought down I have been urged by my friends around me to have this item reclassified so that these new machines could -come in under th-e lower rate of duty. I have been urged by the hon. gentlemen opposite to do the same thing. We have taken it up with the Department -of National Revenue, and although that department was willing to meet the wishes of all concerned, they were confronted by a section which has -been in the act since 1907. Section 59 of the act reads as follows:
If any non-enumerated article equally resembles two or more enumerated articles on

which different rates of duty are chargeable, tlie duty on such non-enumerated article shall be the same as that on the enumerated article which it resembles, paying the highest duty.
They claimed that under that section they were compelled to charge the highest duty.

It is enumerated under
445.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friends are all in
favour of having the duty reduced, so I will ask that the item stand and I will give the officers instructions to amend this act. It cannot be done just by putting in the word "combine"; we must take it out of the classification it is in.
Is there any machine coming in under item 445 which is designated as a harvester, or is there any machine which more clearly fills the bill than that which has the nickname of "combine"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will have to direct that question to the Department of National Revenue, and they probably will be in a position to answer it to-morrow.
Perhaps this hybrid machine was mixed up with the hybrid ticket.

I regret that I was not present during the discussion, but I heard enough from the hon. leader of the opposition to be rather surprised at the language he used in attributing certain things to me, and even presuming to read my thoughts.
Impossible.

I will agree with him there.
I do not pretend to be an expert in interpreting the word "harvester". During the course of the investigation into the Customs department, held some time ago, the minister was criticized for taking upon himself the powers which should be exercised by the heads of the departments. This matter came up through the representations of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher). I am in sympathy with what he would like to have done, and I do not see any reason why a combine should be treated any differently from any other piece of agricultural machinery. The matter was presented to the Commissioner of Customs, who pointed out that it was not a harvester in the strict sense of the interpretation of that word, because it was a combination of two different machines. In that case, as the Minister of Finance has pointed out, you must take the higher rate as applying.

Will the minister tell
us what is meant in item 445 by these words: Mowing machines, harvesters, self-binding or without binders, binding attachments, reapers, and complete parts thereof.
What is meant by the word "harvesters"?
It certainly is not a self-binding reaper.

For example, the old reaper
was called a harvester.
The word "reapers" is here.

I do not pretend to be an expert on the nomenclature of agricultural machinery, but there are machines which are used in the business of agriculture and known as harvesters, and that description does not necessarily apply to a machine which is a combination of two other machines.
What are they?
A binder is a harvester.
My hon. friend is quibbling, absolutely. The word "reaper" is mentioned: the self-binder harvester is mentioned, but still the word " harvester " stands alone.
It is a harvester without a selfJbinder.
What is a harvester without a self-binder?
A reaper.

The reaper is mentioned.
The harvester is a machine that, to my knowledge, has been used in Oregon, Washington, California, for twenty-five years.
I think I have the floor.

Yes, but I asked the
minister if he would interpret that word, and he cannot.

If there is a difference of
opinion in this committee id regard to agricultural machinery, we are not experts with the exception of my hon. friends across the floor to the right, and some on this side; but I will concede that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the leader of the opposition and myself are not experts in naming agricultural machinery. I admit I am not. When the question is one of the interpretation of a tariff item, I am quite willing to leave the interpretation pretty much to those who are particularly charged with that duty.
